title: Winemaking in Depth
description: Every decision in the winery, from sulphur and yeast to extraction, oak and stabilisation.
L: Explain why hygiene matters in the winery

Most wine faults start with poor hygiene. Bacteria and wild yeasts like Brettanomyces live in dirty pipes, pumps and barrels. Wineries clean with hot water, steam, ozone and food-safe chemicals. Barrels are hardest to clean because microbes hide in the wood, which is one reason they are replaced every few years.
Most faults start with dirty equipment

Sulphur dioxide, SO2, has been used since Roman times. It is an antioxidant, binding oxygen and preventing browning. It is antimicrobial, stopping unwanted bacteria and yeasts. Part of it binds to other compounds and stops working; the active part is called free SO2. The total, bound plus free, is regulated: in the EU 150 mg/l for dry reds and 200 mg/l for dry whites.
Why do winemakers measure free SO2 rather than total SO2 to judge protection?
Free SO2 is the active, protective part
Bound SO2 no longer protects. Free SO2 is what fights oxygen and microbes.

Sulphur's effect depends on pH. At low pH, more acidic wines, a much larger share of free SO2 is in its active molecular form. So a high-pH wine needs much more sulphur for the same protection. This is one reason low-acid wines from hot climates can be more fragile.
A wine with higher pH needs more SO2 for the same level of protection.
Yes. At higher pH less free SO2 is in the active molecular form, so more must be added.
SO2 is both antioxidant and antimicrobial
Free SO2 is the active part, and works better at low pH
Explain the risks of stuck fermentation

Ambient, or wild, fermentations start with yeasts from the vineyard and winery. Several species work at first; Saccharomyces cerevisiae takes over as alcohol rises. The result can be more complex, but slower and less predictable. Inoculated fermentations use a selected strain, giving speed, reliability and sometimes specific aromas.

A fermentation sticks when yeast stops before the sugar is gone. Causes include high sugar and alcohol, too high or too low temperatures, and low yeast nutrients, especially nitrogen. A stuck wine is open to spoilage. Winemakers add nutrients, control temperature and, if needed, restart with a strong yeast strain.
Heat, sugar and hunger stop yeast
Which can cause a stuck fermentation?
Too much acidity in the cellar air
High sugar and alcohol, nutrient shortage and extreme temperatures stress yeast.

Yeast does more than make alcohol. It releases aromatic compounds from the grape, like the thiols of Sauvignon Blanc, and creates esters, which smell of banana, pear drop and fruit, especially in cool fermentations. Some yeasts produce more glycerol, adding a smoother texture.
Which aroma is typical of esters from a cool fermentation?
Esters smell of fruit drops and banana, and are common in young, cool-fermented whites and rosés.
Ambient yeast adds complexity; selected yeast adds control
Stuck fermentations come from stress, often heat, sugar or lack of nitrogen
Yeast creates esters and releases grape aromas
Explain cold soak and extended maceration

Extraction can happen before fermentation, as cold soak, where crushed grapes sit cool for days to draw out colour and fruit in water, not alcohol. During fermentation, cap management does the work. After fermentation, extended maceration keeps wine on skins for days or weeks, softening and polymerising tannins.
Cold soak, cap management, extended maceration

Alcohol dissolves tannin more easily than water, so most tannin is extracted later in fermentation. Higher temperatures, 28 to 32 degrees, extract more. Extended maceration, often used for Bordeaux and Barolo, lets short tannins bind into longer chains, which feel softer on the palate.
Why is a cold soak done before fermentation?
To extract colour and fruit without much tannin
Cold soak happens in water, not alcohol, so it extracts colour and fruit aromas but little tannin.

Some winemakers ferment with whole bunches, stems included. Part of the fermentation happens inside intact berries, giving fresh, floral, spicy notes. Ripe stems add tannin and structure and can lower colour and acidity slightly. It is common in Burgundy, the northern Rhône and among many modern producers of Pinot Noir and Syrah.
Match each technique to its timing.
Extraction is planned across the whole process.
Extraction happens before, during and after fermentation
Heat and alcohol extract more tannin
Whole bunches add freshness, spice and structure
Compare protective and oxidative white winemaking
Explain the role of skin contact and solids

To keep fresh, primary fruit, winemakers work protectively: cold grapes, fast pressing, inert gas, SO2, clear juice, cool fermentation in steel. This suits aromatic varieties like Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling. The aim is purity and crispness.

Some winemakers let the juice brown deliberately, called hyperoxidation, so unstable compounds drop out and the wine becomes more resistant to later oxidation. Others ferment cloudier juice with more solids, which adds texture and complexity. These choices suit Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc more than aromatic grapes.
Which grape is most likely to be made protectively to preserve its aromas?
Sauvignon Blanc relies on fresh, volatile aromas, so it is usually handled protectively.

Texture comes from several tools. Barrel fermentation adds richness. Lees contact, especially with stirring, called bâtonnage, releases compounds that add creaminess and protect against oxygen. Skin contact adds phenolics and grip. Malolactic conversion lowers acidity and rounds the wine.
Which techniques add texture to a white wine?
Very clear juice in steel keeps the wine crisp and pure, not textured.
Protective winemaking keeps aromatic whites fresh and pure
Oxidative handling and cloudy juice build resilience and complexity
Lees, barrels, skins and malolactic add texture
Explain when it is used or blocked
Explain the effect of lees ageing

Malolactic conversion, often called malolactic fermentation, is carried out by lactic acid bacteria, mainly Oenococcus oeni. They turn sharp malic acid, found in green apples, into softer lactic acid, found in milk. Acidity falls and the wine feels rounder. A by-product, diacetyl, smells of butter.

Almost all red wines go through malolactic, making them softer and more stable, since bacteria can't later restart in the bottle. For whites, it is a choice. Burgundy Chardonnay usually goes through it; aromatic whites like Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc usually don't. Winemakers block it with SO2, cold temperatures or filtration.
Reds: almost always. Whites: a choice.
Malolactic conversion turns malic acid into ____ acid.
Lactic acid is softer than malic acid. Acetic acid is vinegar, a fault.

Lees are dead yeast cells. Left in contact with the wine, they break down, a process called autolysis, releasing compounds that add creamy texture, bready flavours and protection against oxidation. Muscadet sur lie, white Burgundy and traditional method sparkling wines all rely on it.
Why might a winemaker block malolactic conversion in a Riesling?
To keep its sharp acidity and pure fruit
Riesling relies on crisp acidity and pure fruit. Malolactic would soften it and add buttery notes.
Malolactic turns malic acid into softer lactic acid
It's standard in reds and a choice in whites
Lees ageing adds creaminess, bready notes and protection
Explain the effect of barrel size and age
Compare French, American and other oaks

Smaller barrels have more wood surface per litre, so they add more flavour and oxygen. A 225-litre barrique gives much more effect than a 500-litre puncheon or a 2,000-litre foudre. New barrels give the most flavour; after three or four fills they are called neutral, giving oxygen but little flavour.

French oak, mainly from forests like Tronçais and Allier, has tight grain and gives fine tannins and subtle spice. American oak, Quercus alba, gives more vanilla and coconut, from compounds called lactones. Staves are often seasoned outdoors for two to three years to soften harsh tannins. Eastern European oak offers a cheaper, French-like alternative.
French: subtle. American: coconut and vanilla.
Match each choice to its result.
Barrel size, origin and toast each change the result.

Barrels are bent over fire, which toasts the inside. Light toast keeps more wood tannin and gives fresh oak notes. Medium toast gives vanilla, caramel and spice. Heavy toast gives coffee, smoke and roasted notes, and less oak tannin. Toast is ordered to suit the wine.
A neutral barrel adds no oxygen to the wine.
Not true. A neutral barrel adds little flavour, but still lets small amounts of oxygen in through the wood and joints.
Small, new barrels have the strongest effect
French oak is subtle; American oak gives coconut and vanilla
Toast level shapes flavours from fresh wood to smoke

Fining agents bind unwanted particles or compounds, then settle out: bentonite clay removes proteins; egg white or gelatin softens tannins; PVPP removes browning compounds. Filtration physically removes particles; a sterile filter removes yeast and bacteria. Some producers avoid both, arguing they strip flavour.

Whites can turn hazy in warm conditions if proteins are unstable; bentonite fixes it. Tartrate crystals form in cold; cold stabilisation chills the wine to about minus 4 degrees so crystals drop out before bottling. Microbial stability matters most for wines with sugar or no malolactic, which are usually sterile filtered.
Bentonite for protein; cold for tartrates
What does bentonite remove from white wine?
Bentonite, a clay, binds proteins that could otherwise cause haze in warm conditions.

Bottling is a risky moment: wine can pick up oxygen or microbes. Lines are sterilised, bottles flushed with inert gas, and dissolved oxygen measured. The closure is chosen for the wine's life: natural cork, technical cork, screw cap or glass. Many wines then rest in bottle before release.
Which wines are most likely to be sterile filtered?
Residual sugar and malic acid could feed microbes in the bottle. Dry reds after malolactic are more stable.
Fining binds particles; filtration removes them
Bentonite fixes protein haze; cold stabilisation drops tartrates
Bottling must avoid oxygen and microbes
What is the active, protective form of sulphur dioxide?
Free SO2 does the work; bound SO2 no longer protects.
Match each technique to its purpose.
Each tool solves a specific problem.
Which are common causes of a stuck fermentation?
Too much oxygen in the bottle
Stress from nutrients, heat or sugar stops yeast.
Almost all red wines go through malolactic conversion.
Yes. It softens them and makes them more stable in bottle.
Order these barrels from strongest to weakest oak effect.
Smaller and newer means more flavour; larger and older means less.
Hygiene and SO2 protect wine from microbes and oxygen
Extraction and texture are shaped by temperature, time, lees and malolactic
Oak size, origin, age and toast decide its effect
Fining, filtration and stabilisation prepare wine for the bottle
